title: GPU network topology and tenant isolation patterns
author: Ava Lin
body:
Overview:

This document captures the recommended network topology patterns, Terraform contracts, CI/CD build hooks, and runbook steps we use to provision and operate GPU-enabled clusters across accounts and regions. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Goals:
- Provide tenant isolation patterns that minimize blast radius while preserving GPU utilization efficiency.
- Define Terraform module contracts and interfaces for VPC, subnets, and interconnects used by GPU fleets.
- Document CI/CD and node-bootstrap integration points so GPU images and kernel modules deploy consistently.
- Provide concrete runbook steps for network-related GPU incidents (e.g., connectivity loss, degraded throughput).

Audience and scope:
- Audience: infra engineers, cloud networking, SRE, platform team.
- Scope: multi-account VPCs, dedicated GPU subnets, egress controls, Transit/Peering patterns, Terraform modules, and bootstrap CI/CD pipelines. Does NOT cover model-serving runtime internals (see eng-serving-runtime docs).

High-level topology patterns (textual diagram):

Pattern A — Tenant-dedicated VPC with shared interconnect
- Each tenant gets a dedicated VPC containing management subnets and a dedicated GPU-subnet (private).
- A central shared services VPC hosts NAT/egress, logging, and ISP-facing egress gateways.
- Interconnect implemented via Transit Gateway (AWS) / Cloud Router + Dedicated Interconnect (GCP) or VPC Peering for smaller orgs.

Pattern B — Shared compute VPC with tenant routing (cost optimized)
- One compute VPC contains GPU pools across AZs. Tenants isolated using route tables + security groups + VRF-equivalent constructs.
- Works best for high-density usage where tenants are trusted and SLA boundaries are contractual rather than enforced at network layer.

Pattern C — Hybrid on-prem + cloud attach for Private deployments
- On-prem data center has an isolated GPU VLAN and is connected to cloud via HA VPN or Direct Connect.
- Control plane lives in customer-managed VPC with restricted ingress.

Trade-offs summary:
- Pattern A: maximum isolation, slightly higher operational cost and cross-VPC routing latency.
- Pattern B: lower cost, higher risk of noisy neighbor, requires stricter tenant scheduling.
- Pattern C: necessary for regulated customers; requires careful key management and audit logging.

Terraform module contracts:

We maintain a set of canonical modules under the terraform registry: redwood/gpu-vpc, redwood/gpu-subnet, redwood/gpu-interconnect, redwood/gpu-nat-gateway. The expected input/output contract for gpu-subnet is: 
- inputs: name, cidr_block, availability_zones, allowed_tenants (list of account IDs or tenant tag selectors), kube_node_labels (map), taints (list)
- outputs: subnet_id, route_table_id, security_group_ids

Example usage (AWS-style pseudocode):

```
module "gpu_subnet_tenant_alpha" {
  source = "registry.redwood/gpu-subnet"
  name = "alpha-gpu-subnet"
  cidr_block = "10.40.128.0/24"
  availability_zones = ["us-west-2a","us-west-2b"]
  allowed_tenants = ["111122223333"]
  kube_node_labels = { workload = "gpu", tier = "inference" }
  taints = ["gpu:true:NoSchedule"]
}
```

Network security controls:
- Security groups: minimal egress restrictions for control plane and ephemeral egress for OS packs. Allow kubelet, kube-proxy, and SSH from jump hosts only.
- Route table hygiene: GPU subnets must have explicit routes to NAT gateways in shared services VPC and to Transit Gateway attachments.
- Egress monitoring: All GPU subnets must export flow logs to the central logging account; retain for 90 days by default.

GKE / Kubernetes node bootstrap and CI/CD hooks:

Image pipeline notes:
1) GPU node images are built in the gpu-image CI pipeline. The pipeline produces AMIs/GCP images and publishes a signed manifest to the artifact registry.
2) Image pipeline steps: base image -> kernel + nvidia drivers -> runtime deps -> auditing agent -> image signing.
3) Image promotion stages: build -> canary -> promoted. Canary is a single node-pool in a non-prod namespace.

Example node bootstrap snippet (init script):

```
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# install nvidia drivers (package manager or runcontainer)
apt-get update && apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-530
# configure kubelet labels/taints (labels from instance metadata)
/usr/local/bin/rdw-kube-labeler --labels "gpu=true,tier=inference" --taints "gpu=true:NoSchedule"
# register with cluster and join nodepool
kubeadm join --token ${TOKEN} ${CONTROL_PLANE} --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:${HASH}
```

CI/CD integration points:
- Terraform PRs that change network topology require a gated plan + approval from networking owners.
- Image CI must publish the signed manifest before the nodepool autoscaler can adopt the new image.
- A GitHub Actions job (or Jenkins) runs terraform fmt/validate/plan and posts a drift check comment on PRs.

Autoscaling and spot/interrupt handling:
- GPU node pools use a mix of on-demand and spot. Default ratio: 70% on-demand for critical tiers, 30% spot for batch workloads.
- Use a spot-fallback autoscaler that will spin replacement on-demand instances if spot reclaim rate > 2% within a 5-minute window.
- Batching workloads should be routed to dedicated spot node pools and labeled "spot-batch".

Monitoring and alerting (recommended metrics & thresholds):
- VPC connectivity: Transit attachment health — alert if >1 attachment is Unavailable for >2m.
- Egress saturation: NAT gateway dropped packets > 0.5% over 5m -> P2.
- Packet loss from control plane to GPU nodes > 1% over 3m -> P1.
- Flow log missing for a subnet -> P1 (indicates config or retention failure).

Runbook: GPU network incident (connectivity loss / high packet loss)
1) Triage and ownership:
   - Pager to infra-networking on-call.
   - Acknowledge in incident channel and create incident page with start time.
2) Quick checks (first 5 minutes):
   - Verify Transit Gateway / Cloud Router status in cloud console.
   - Check flow logs for GPU subnet for recent drops.
   - Check BGP sessions (if DirectConnect/Interconnect) for down state.
3) Mitigation steps:
   - If Transit attachment is Detached: reattach via console or terraform apply plan (owner: network-ops).
   - If NAT gateway saturated: provision additional NATs in same AZ and update route table to use failover.
   - If kernel-level packet drop on node: cordon node, drain non-critical pods, boot a fresh node from promoted image.
4) Rollback and communication:
   - If a Terraform change caused the issue, revert the merge and re-run apply from the last known good plan.
   - Communicate to customers with ETA and mitigation steps; update incident page every 15 minutes.
5) Post-incident:
   - Root cause analysis within 48 hours.
   - Recoverability test: create synthetic traffic across attachment and ensure 99.5% success at 95th percentile.

Ownership and contacts:
- Network-ops: primary owner for topology changes and transit attachments.
- GPU-fleet: owner for node images and autoscaler behaviors.
- SRE: alerting and incident coordination.
- On-call rotation: see /confluence/eng-infra/eng-sre/oncall-rotations for schedules.

Compatibility matrix (non-exhaustive):
- AWS: Transit Gateway + TGW attachments supported; use ENI offload with latest AMIs.
- GCP: Shared VPC with Private Google Access; use Alias IPs for pod networking.
- Azure: Use Virtual WAN for multi-region attach; GPU SKUs require accelerated networking.

Security and compliance items:
- Key management: KMS keys for image signing and for disk encryption; access limited to build service principal.
- Audit logs: Enable cloud Audit Logging for route table and security group changes; forward to central SIEM and retain 1 year for critical customers.
- RBAC: Terraform state apply guardians must be in the infra-admins group; plan-only reviewers can be infra-engineers.

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets and checks
- Check Transit attachments (AWS): aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments --filters Name=resource-type,Values=vpc
- Check BGP sessions (GCP): gcloud compute routers get-status ${ROUTER_NAME} --region=${REGION}
- Verify flow logs exist: aws ec2 describe-flow-logs --filter Name=resource-id,Values=${SUBNET_ID}
